0: Region-Dependent Transfer in an Exposure-Matched Cross-Event Coseismic Landslide Segmentation Benchmark
2: Coseismic landslide inventories support post-earthquake response, but models trained and validated within one earthquake may not transfer to unseen regions. We built a controlled cross-region benchmark from the CAS Landslide Dataset with seven held-out regions (six coseismic and one rainfall-triggered), four architectures and three seeds. The benchmark evaluates a supplied positive-tile distribution and does not estimate complete-event or prospective performance. Source validation IoU ranged from 0.593 to 0.719, whereas cross-region macro IoU fell to 0.157-0.181, retaining only 22.9%-30.5% of in-domain accuracy; SegFormer-B0 had the lowest source IoU but the highest cross-region IoU at every threshold from 0.3 to 0.7. Source expansion changed performance by region. An epoch-matched comparison was confounded by 6.34x greater exposure in the pooled regime. Under exposure-matched training, pooled source minus the source-only replay placebo changed target macro IoU by +0.0355 [-0.0005, +0.0948] in a tile-cluster bootstrap and increased MCC by +0.0851 [+0.0015, +0.2308], while the balanced-IoU interval crossed zero. Hokkaido showed a robust gain across overlap and prevalence-robust endpoints, Palu a small +0.0066 IoU effect below the reporting marker, and Lombok no IoU change but opposite changes in precision, recall and HD95. The temporal early-peak pattern appeared in only two of six replication runs and is not treated as a stable mechanism. Adapting ResUNet with 20 labelled target tiles produced a precision-led benchmark gain, raising macro IoU on the three most difficult events from 0.049 to 0.181. The gain persisted under 256/512 m support-query buffers, alternative support draws, and a query-covered stitched-map check, but recall did not improve and Palu HD95 worsened. Adaptation reduced Brier score and high-confidence error, although target calibration remained substantially worse than source calibration. Within the tested models, regions and budget, source expansion must be evaluated per region and the few-shot result is a bounded benchmark improvement rather than evidence of operational readiness.

33: Training uses 50 epochs for the source-only runs and 20 continuation epochs for the control and transfer runs, with a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 1 x 10-4, weight decay of 1 x 10-4, mixed precision, and the PolyGHMDiceLoss objective. Checkpoint selection uses the source validation split only; no target imagery influences training or model selection. The exposure-matched pooled treatment contains 1,795 CAS tiles, 5,925 Jiuzhai Valley tiles, 2,504 Longxi River tiles, 980 Moxitaidi tiles and 178 Wenchuan tiles, for 11,382 training tiles across five domain slots. WeightedRandomSampler assigns sample weight 1/n_domain, so each domain has 0.20 expected sampling mass and an expected 7,168 image exposures at the common budget of 35,840 exposures. The source-only replay placebo uses five copies of the CAS stream with the same 0.20 mass per slot. All experiments ran on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU with 8 GB of memory, and were executed serially.
34: Segmentation accuracy is reported as IoU and Dice at a fixed decision threshold of 0.5, and boundary quality as boundary F1 at tolerances of 2 and 4 pixels and as the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance. Balanced IoU and MCC are co-primary prevalence-robust endpoints. We report IoU at five decision thresholds from 0.3 to 0.7 together with macro precision and recall at 0.5, because IoU is sensitive to class prevalence and the regions differ in foreground fraction by nearly a factor of 20; the sweep and its implications are reported in Section 4.11. Retention is defined as the ratio of cross-event macro IoU to source validation IoU. The two quantities are aggregated differently, an unweighted mean over seven regions against a single source-validation score, so retention is descriptive and not an inferential statistic. Region-level transfer is reported as the difference in IoU between the multi-source model and the source-only model evaluated on the same region. Few-shot robustness was evaluated on the same adapted checkpoints after excluding query tiles within a GSD-aware 256 or 512 m physical buffer of any support tile, at thresholds from 0.3 to 0.7, and on a seed-42 stitched map over the union of query-chip pixels. Three deterministic support draws were trained separately with the source initialization fixed. ECE, Brier score and risk-coverage were recomputed from frozen checkpoints without further training.
36: The unit of analysis is the region, not the pixel. Pixel-level testing would inflate the sample size and treat spatially correlated pixels as independent observations. Transfer values are computed at the region level, and paired contrasts resample target regions, seeds and tiles within each region-seed stratum. The source-expansion and few-shot analyses use 10,000 bootstrap draws. We use an absolute IoU difference of 0.01 as a reporting marker on the bounded 0-1 IoU scale; it is not a deployment threshold. A headline claim additionally requires an interval excluding zero and directional support from a prevalence-robust endpoint. Boundary F1 is reported from the region-seed hierarchical bootstrap because per-tile boundary extraction was not available for the full replication set. This is a reporting convention rather than a significance test: with three seeds per configuration and a small number of regions, conventional null-hypothesis testing has insufficient power, so per-seed and per-region consistency are reported alongside intervals.
38: Because the few-shot results depend on the separation between support and query tiles, we audited spatial overlap directly. Source training and validation contain no exact image or mask duplicates and no strong perceptual near-duplicates under joint perceptual-hash, structural-similarity and mask-overlap review. The target regions contain no duplicate images. For every few-shot seed and region, the minimum Chebyshev distance between support and query chips is 2 in the reconstructed stride-256 grid, with no pairs at distance 1 or less. The split guarantees that chips do not overlap, but it does not guarantee a buffer, and support and query remain samples from the same annotation inventory rather than independently annotated validation sets. Imposing an additional 256 m buffer would retain 86% of the Hokkaido query chips, 61 to 66% of the Lombok chips and 92 to 93% of the Palu chips. We therefore re-evaluated the same adapted checkpoints under 0, 256 and 512 m buffers and with three deterministic support draws (Section 4.8). Spatial adjacency among the variable-sized source training and validation images cannot be reconstructed from their filenames, so partial overlap in the source split cannot be excluded. Source rasters also lack CRS and geotransform metadata, so source spatial independence is not claimed.
133: The source-fraction ablation raises source validation IoU without producing a monotonic target gain, so source fit and transfer are not interchangeable. The exposure-matched test then shows that the pooled treatment changes performance by region, with a large Hokkaido effect, a small Palu effect and no IoU change on Lombok. These results indicate that added regions are neither uniformly beneficial nor uniformly harmful under the tested pipeline.
134: The source-target divergence is the more robust observation than any single temporal mechanism. Additional source data and stronger augmentation did not remove that divergence, but the pre-specified early-peak pattern failed replication and is therefore reported as a model-specific observation rather than a general source-overfitting mechanism.
136: Two benchmark-level consequences follow. First, a single aggregate transfer score is not sufficient for deciding whether to pool data: transfer must be reported per target region because both sign and metric direction can differ. Second, because source-domain ranking does not reliably predict cross-event ranking, architecture selection on in-domain validation can choose the wrong model. The cross-event benchmark is therefore the relevant selection criterion within the tested tile distribution. These results do not establish complete-map behaviour, annotation requirements in an operational workflow, or performance on a future earthquake.
137: Among the tested benchmark interventions, few-shot adaptation with 20 labelled target tiles produced the largest and most consistent improvement in overlap metrics, raising macro IoU on the three most difficult events from 0.049 to 0.181 for ResUNet. This statement covers two adaptation depths, three target regions and one budget of 400 optimiser steps, and the evaluation uses a guarded query set and a query-covered stitched map rather than complete event maps. Within that scope, the gain persisted under 256 and 512 m support-query buffers, alternative support draws, and a seed-42 stitched-map check. The gain was precision-led: recall did not improve, and Palu HD95 worsened. Decoder-only fine-tuning had lower cross-seed variance than full fine-tuning but weaker mean gains in Lombok and Palu. The result therefore supports a bounded benchmark comparison, not a claim that 20 tiles are sufficient for emergency mapping.
142: The interpretation is bounded by the supplied tile distribution and independent of claims that the data cannot support. First, all target samples are positive 512-pixel chips. Complete-event mosaics, stable-slope negatives, false-positive area, omitted area and full-map precision are unavailable, so the study does not support complete-map or emergency-readiness claims. Second, source rasters have no CRS, geotransform, scene identifiers or tile polygons. Source training and validation independence cannot be established, and source-to-target geographic distances cannot be quantified. Third, the few-shot query set is a label holdout from the same annotation inventory as the support tiles; it is not an independently annotated validation partition. Fourth, no chronological or post-cutoff event is available, so prospective and next-earthquake generalisation are not tested. Fifth, the seven target regions differ in annotation convention, sensor, GSD and acquisition timing, with GSD spanning 0.2 to 5 m and acquisition dates spanning 2008 to 2022. GSD and landslide prevalence are collinear across regions and cannot be separated causally. Sixth, the primary benchmark uses 128 x 128 inputs and the 256 experiment resizes the same 512 tiles; native-resolution training and inference remain untested.
143: The intervention-specific boundaries are equally important. The exposure-matched causal contrast covers one architecture, three target regions and one training budget. Its tile-cluster Macro IoU interval crosses zero, the balanced-IoU interval crosses zero, and MCC is the robust co-primary endpoint; the result therefore supports region-dependent change rather than a uniformly positive source-diversity effect. Hokkaido has a robust positive effect, Palu is below the 0.01 reporting marker, and Lombok has no IoU change despite opposite changes in precision, recall, balanced IoU and HD95. The temporal early-peak pattern replicated in only two of six runs and is not treated as a mechanism. The few-shot robustness panel covers ResUNet and one adaptation budget. Calibration and ECE are post-hoc diagnostics and do not establish deployment reliability. Finally, public release still requires an author-approved code license, repository owner and persistent identifier.
145: In a controlled cross-event benchmark of coseismic landslide segmentation, models trained on source areas retained only 22.9% to 30.5% of their in-domain IoU on seven held-out regions, and in-domain ranking did not reliably predict cross-event ranking. The epoch-matched pooled comparison was confounded by 6.34 times greater exposure. With exposure matched, pooled source versus the source-only replay placebo changed target macro IoU by +0.0355 [-0.0005, +0.0948] in a tile-cluster bootstrap and increased MCC by +0.0851 [+0.0015, +0.2308]; the balanced-IoU interval crossed zero. The effect was region-dependent: Hokkaido improved robustly across overlap and prevalence-robust endpoints, Palu improved slightly below the reporting marker, and Lombok showed no IoU change. Across seven regions, accuracy tracked the reference foreground fraction (Spearman 0.93), but the association was precision-led, so part of the regional difficulty measured by IoU reflects the metric rather than segmentation alone. The replay placebo showed that the multi-stream input format itself contributed little. The early-peak source-overfitting pattern appeared in only two of six replication runs and is not treated as a general mechanism. Adapting ResUNet with 20 labelled target tiles produced a precision-led benchmark improvement, raising macro IoU on the three most difficult events from 0.049 to 0.181; recall did not improve and Palu HD95 worsened. Within the tested models, regions and budget, these results support per-region validation of source expansion and a bounded tile-level few-shot comparison, not complete-map deployment or next-earthquake readiness.
147: The CAS Landslide Dataset is openly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10294997 and is described by Xu et al. (2024). The imagery for Lombok and Palu is distributed under CC BY-NC 4.0, which restricts redistribution, so those tiles should be obtained from the original source rather than from this study. The region manifest, split assignments, per-seed evaluation outputs, few-shot assignments, calibration outputs and metric implementations used here have been assembled into a versioned release candidate. Before submission, the authors will select the code license, make the repository public, archive the tagged release, and insert its persistent identifier at this location. Trained model checkpoints are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
